questions.q: The orders API and the checkout each had their own copy of OrderStatus. Why did neither compiler catch the missing "refunded" label?
questions.explain: Types protect a contract only where one compiler sees both sides. With one owner package imported everywhere, adding a status breaks every incomplete Record<OrderStatus, string> in the same commit.
options: The checkout used JavaScript, not TypeScript
Each compiler only checked its own repository against its own copy of the type; no compiler ever saw both sides of the contract
Record types are not checked for missing keys
JSON.parse always returns a string

questions.q: Two copies of a status type have drifted apart. What does this print?
questions.explain: labels["refunded"] is undefined at runtime, so the ?? fallback shows it. The compiler believed the as and saw no problem; only a shared type would have exposed the missing label.
options: Paid | ?refunded | Awaiting payment
Paid | undefined | Awaiting payment
Paid | refunded | Awaiting payment
Paid | Awaiting payment

questions.q: After npm install in a workspace, what is node_modules/@shop/core?
questions.explain: Workspaces link local packages. A change in packages/core is visible through the link immediately, although dependents still read core's built output through its exports map.
options: A copy of the @shop/core tarball from the npm registry
A symbolic link to the packages/core folder
An empty folder that TypeScript fills during the build
A copy of packages/core/src

questions.q: In the shop monorepo, @shop/database imports "@shop/core". Which core files does the compiler read to check database?
questions.explain: The link leads to core's package.json, whose "types" condition points into dist. That is why build order matters, and why project references exist.
options: packages/core/src/index.ts, through the workspace link
packages/core/dist/index.d.ts, found through core's exports map, so core must be built first
Whatever is newer, the source or the declaration
Nothing: internal packages are not type-checked

questions.q: Which of these does "composite": true NOT require or imply?
questions.explain: composite is about being referenced by other projects: declarations, a complete file list and incremental information. Publishing is unrelated; internal packages are usually "private": true.
options: declaration output, because dependents read your .d.ts files
Every source file matched by include or files
Incremental build information in a .tsbuildinfo file
That the project is published to npm

questions.q: Why do the shop packages (and ZudoJS's) set "tsBuildInfoFile": "dist/.tsbuildinfo"?
questions.explain: Incremental builds trust the .tsbuildinfo file. If "clean" removes dist but leaves that file elsewhere, the next build can skip emitting and still exit with 0.
options: TypeScript refuses to build without it
So that deleting dist also deletes the build information; otherwise a stale .tsbuildinfo can make the next build think everything is current and emit nothing
So that the build information is published to npm
It makes the build faster than the default location

questions.q: What is the root tsconfig.json with "files": [] and a references list for?
questions.explain: tsc -b at the root follows the references to every package and builds them in order. "files": [] prevents the root from also compiling every .ts file it can see as one big project.
options: It compiles all packages into one output folder
It is a solution file: it compiles nothing itself and lets tsc -b (and editors) find every project
It disables type checking for the packages
It is required by npm workspaces

questions.q: What does tsc -b do that tsc -p packages/http does not?
questions.explain: -b turns tsc into a build orchestrator over the reference graph. -p compiles one project and expects its dependencies' declarations to exist already.
options: It type-checks more strictly
It builds referenced projects first, in dependency order, and skips projects that are up to date
It bundles all packages into one file
It publishes the packages

questions.q: tsc -b --verbose says a dependent is "up to date with .d.ts files from its dependencies" and only updates its output timestamps. What changed?
questions.explain: A change inside a function body changes a package's .js but not its .d.ts. Dependents only see declarations, so their result cannot change.
options: Nothing at all
A dependency was rebuilt, but its declaration files came out identical, so the dependent does not need to be checked again
The dependent's own source changed
The dependent's tsconfig.json changed

questions.q: You add a JSDoc comment to the exported Logger interface. Why does tsc -b rebuild database, auth and http?
questions.explain: The decision is made by comparing declaration output. Even a comment counts, because it is part of the .d.ts file (and useful to users on hover).
options: Every change always rebuilds every dependent
Comments are copied into .d.ts files, so logger's declarations changed, and dependents are rebuilt when a dependency's declarations change
JSDoc comments change the JavaScript output
The comment made the build information invalid

questions.q: http imports @shop/auth and lists it in package.json, but its tsconfig.json has no reference to ../auth. What happens?
questions.explain: tsc -b only knows the reference graph. Without the reference, auth is not in http's build at all, and its dist/index.d.ts does not exist when http is compiled.
options: The compiler reports a missing reference by name
Building from the root may still work if the solution happens to build auth earlier; building http alone from clean fails with TS2307, because auth is never built
It always works, because npm linked auth
TypeScript builds auth automatically because of package.json

questions.q: What does error TS6202, "Project references may not form a circular graph", tell you to do?
questions.explain: Two projects that need each other's declarations cannot be built in any order. The fix is a design change, not a build trick.
options: Add "composite": false to one of the projects
Build the two projects twice
Remove the cycle: move the shared piece into a lower package or pass plain data across the boundary, so the dependency points one way
Merge the reference lists of both projects

questions.q: database imports "../../core/src/index.js" instead of "@shop/core", and database references core. What does the lesson show happens?
questions.explain: The emitted JavaScript keeps the relative path, which points at a folder with only .ts files. Without the reference the compiler reports TS6059/TS6307 instead. Import across packages by name only.
options: TS6059 and TS6307 errors
The build passes (the compiler maps the source to core's declarations), but at runtime Node.js cannot find packages/core/src/index.js
It works both at compile time and at runtime
Node.js follows the workspace link instead

questions.q: What is a phantom dependency?
questions.explain: It works while the accident holds: a previous build left output, or the installer hoisted the package. On a clean build, with pnpm, or after publishing, it fails.
options: A dependency listed in package.json but never imported
A package that code imports without declaring it, which resolves only by accident, for example through npm's root node_modules links
A dependency that is only used in types
A package that was unpublished from the registry

questions.q: With a phantom import of @shop/auth in database, the lesson's clean build failed and the next build passed. Why is that the worst outcome?
questions.explain: An order-dependent build depends on leftovers. CI should always build from clean, and the real fix is to declare the dependency (and its reference), or remove the import.
options: Because the second build is slower
Because it fails on clean machines such as CI and passes on laptops that already have dist folders, so it is hard to reproduce and easy to dismiss
Because TypeScript deletes auth's output
Because npm uninstalls auth

questions.q: Why does pnpm turn the phantom dependency into an error on every machine?
questions.explain: In the lesson, packages/database/node_modules/@shop held only core and logger, and the root had no node_modules/@shop at all, so @shop/auth could not resolve from database.
options: pnpm runs tsc during install
Each package's own node_modules contains only what that package declares, and there are no root links to every workspace package
pnpm refuses to install packages with import type
pnpm deletes dist folders

questions.q: Why does the ZudoJS repository require "workspace:*" for every internal dependency instead of a range such as "0.1.0"?
questions.explain: When ZudoJS pinned its siblings to 0.1.0, a build break, two failing tests and a timer leak stayed hidden until the packages were linked to source. workspace:* can only mean the local folder.
options: Ranges are not allowed in pnpm
A hand-written range can resolve to a published copy from the registry, so packages compile against an old tarball and changes to their siblings are invisible
workspace:* makes installs faster
npm requires it for publishing

questions.q: What happens if you publish a package that depends on "@shop/core": "workspace:*" with plain npm publish?
questions.explain: The workspace protocol is a pnpm (and Yarn) feature. The tool that understands it must also be the one that publishes.
options: npm rewrites it to the current version
The literal text workspace:* is uploaded, and nobody can install the package; pnpm publish rewrites it to a real version
npm refuses to publish scoped packages
The dependency is silently dropped

questions.q: This function mimics how pnpm publish rewrites the workspace protocol. What does it print?
questions.explain: workspace:* becomes the exact current version, workspace:^ becomes a caret range on it, and external ranges pass through untouched. The published package.json only contains real version ranges.
options: { '@shop/core': '*', '@shop/logger': '^', ms: '^2.1.3' }
{ '@shop/core': 'workspace:*', '@shop/logger': 'workspace:^', ms: '^2.1.3' }

questions.q: What does this build-level computation print?
questions.explain: Each round takes every package whose dependencies are all done. payments needs only core, but core is not done until the end of round one, so payments joins round two. Packages in one round can be built in parallel.
options:
core, logger
auth, database, payments
http

core, logger, payments
auth, database
http

core
logger
auth, database, payments
http
http, auth, database, core, logger, payments

questions.q: What does this "affected packages" computation print?
questions.explain: Affected means "depends on the change, directly or indirectly". logger reaches database, and through it http and reports. auth reaches only http; its own dependency core is not affected by a change in auth.
options:
database http logger reports
auth http

database logger
auth http

auth core database http logger reports
auth http

database http logger reports
auth core http

questions.q: The same level computation, on a graph with a cycle. What does it print?
questions.explain: auth and http wait for each other forever, and reports waits behind them. The level method lists everything stuck; finding the actual loop needs a depth-first search, as in the lesson's exercise.
options:
build: core
stuck: auth, http, reports

build: core
stuck: auth, http

build: core, reports
stuck: auth, http
stuck: core, auth, http, reports

questions.q: What does this tier check print?
questions.explain: Same-tier dependencies (auth on database) pass this rule; only depending on a higher tier is reported. Whether same-tier dependencies are allowed is a policy choice: ZudoJS allows them, and relies on the separate cycle check.
options:
database -> http goes up
done

auth -> database goes up
database -> http goes up
done

database -> http goes up
http -> auth goes up
done
done

questions.q: A boundary checker finds imports with a regular expression. What does it report for this source?
questions.explain: The pattern sees every from "…", including import type and export … from, but misses the dynamic import("@shop/http"). That is the limitation the lesson's tip warns about; real tools use the compiler API.
options: @shop/core, @shop/auth, @shop/logger
@shop/core, @shop/auth, @shop/logger, @shop/http
@shop/core, @shop/logger
@shop/core

questions.q: Two different versions of @shop/core ended up installed, and code checks errors from both. What does this print?
questions.explain: Two installed versions are two modules with two classes, like the dual-package hazard. The shop's http would turn a "not found" into a 500. A workspace with workspace:* guarantees a single local copy of each internal package.
options: false ORDER_NOT_FOUND
true ORDER_NOT_FOUND
false undefined
true undefined

questions.q: A tool turns tsconfig reference paths into package names. What does it print?
questions.explain: replace with a string replaces only the first match. The lesson's tool assumes the shop's layout ("../name"); a sturdier version takes the last path segment, for example r.path.split("/").at(-1), or reads the referenced package.json.
options: @shop/core @shop/../packages/logger
@shop/core @shop/logger
@shop/core @shop/packages/logger
@shop/core @shop/../../packages/logger

questions.q: auth produces AuditEvent objects and database stores them. Both are tier 1. Where should the AuditEvent type live?
questions.explain: Putting it in either peer makes the other depend sideways on it. A shared contract belongs below both parties; copying it brings back the drift problem.
options: In auth, which creates them
In database, which stores them
In a lower package both already depend on, such as core (or a new tier-0 package for events)
Copied into both packages

questions.q: The shop's @shop/core has no dependencies, while ZudoJS's @zudojs/core is in tier 2 and depends on many packages. What does that show?
questions.explain: ZudoJS's core wires the framework together, so it sits above what it wires. The shop's core holds shared domain types, so it sits at the bottom. Read the tier map, not the names.
options: One of the two repositories is wrong
A package's name says nothing about its place in the graph; the dependency graph and the tier map do
Packages called core must always be at the top
Tiers only apply to pnpm workspaces

questions.q: Which pnpm command builds @shop/auth and every package that depends on it?
questions.explain: Three dots before the name add its dependents; three dots after add its dependencies. Dependents are what a change can break, so ...@shop/auth is the "affected" selection.
options: pnpm --filter "@shop/auth..." run build
pnpm --filter "...@shop/auth" run build
pnpm -r --only @shop/auth run build
pnpm build @shop/auth

questions.q: Why does the lesson advise against mapping "@shop/*" to source folders with the paths compiler option instead of using packages?
questions.explain: An alias makes every file of every package importable from everywhere. That skips a build step, but it also skips every check this lesson relies on.
options: paths does not work with strict
It bypasses the package boundaries (no exports, no declared dependencies, no references), and Node.js ignores paths, so the runtime needs extra tooling
It makes type checking slower than project references in every case
TypeScript 7 removed paths

questions.q: Why should a monorepo's CI build start from a clean checkout instead of reusing cached dist folders by default?
questions.explain: Every failure in the lesson's phantom dependency and missing reference sections depended on what was, or was not, already built. Caching is fine once it is keyed correctly; the default should be honest.
options: Clean builds produce smaller files
Leftover output hides order problems such as phantom dependencies and missing references, which only fail when nothing is built yet
TypeScript cannot read cached output
npm requires it

questions.q: Write buildLevels(deps): given a map from package to the packages it depends on, return an array of rounds, where each round lists (in map order) every package whose dependencies are all in earlier rounds. Throw Error("cycle") if a round would be empty while packages remain.
questions.explain: This is a topological sort in rounds (Kahn's algorithm, grouped). The rounds are also the parallelism a build tool can use: everything in one round can build at once.

questions.q: Write affected(deps, changed): return the changed package plus every package that depends on it directly or indirectly, sorted alphabetically.
questions.explain: Keep adding any package that needs something already in the set, until a full pass adds nothing. CI uses exactly this to test only what a change can have broken.
questions.expected:
admin auth core database http
admin database http
admin

questions.q: Write tierViolations(tiers, deps) that returns one message "<pkg> (tier N) must not depend on <dep> (tier M)" for every dependency on a higher tier, and "<pkg> has no tier" for a package missing from the tier map (check each package once, before its dependencies).
questions.explain: A package missing from the map must be an error, not a silent tier 0: otherwise any new package could depend on anything. ZudoJS's check fails for an unknown package for the same reason.
questions.expected:
auth (tier 1) must not depend on http (tier 2)
reports has no tier

questions.q: Write undeclaredImports(source, declared, self): find every @shop/… package the source imports, through from "…" or import("…"), and return (sorted, without duplicates) those that are neither declared nor the package itself.
questions.explain: The pattern now also catches dynamic imports. A Set removes the duplicate @shop/auth, and a package importing its own name (self-reference) is not a dependency.

questions.q: Write compareReferences(dependencies, references) that returns { missing, extra }: dependencies without a matching reference, and references without a matching dependency. References are paths like "../core"; take the last path segment as the package folder, and package names are @shop/<folder>.
questions.explain: A missing reference makes builds order-dependent; an extra one makes a package wait for, and rebuild after, something it does not use. Both directions are worth reporting.

questions.q: CI knows which files a pull request changed. Write packagesFor(files) that maps each file under packages/<folder>/ to @shop/<folder> and returns the distinct package names, sorted; files outside packages/ (such as README.md) map to nothing.
questions.explain: Combined with affected, this gives CI the full list to build and test. Changes outside any package (tools, root configs) are the risky case: many teams treat them as "affects everything".

questions.q: Write findCycle(deps) with depth-first search: return the first loop found as a path such as ["auth", "http", "auth"], or null. Visit packages and dependencies in map and array order.
questions.explain: "Visiting" marks nodes on the current path. Meeting one again closes a loop, which is the part of the path from that node onward. "Done" nodes were fully explored without a loop and are skipped.
